newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa funds could live with prudential controls.
newsitem.headline: South Africa funds could live with prudential controls.

text.p: South African funds are pushing for the dismantling of foreign exchange controls but could live with limited prudential controls on their offshore investments, according to industry officials.
Finance Minister Trevor Manuel last week mooted the idea of prudential requirements on institutions to protect pensions and savings even after exchange controls go.
Southern International chief executive Carel de Ridder supported the need to review prudency rules to fit the changed investment environment after the abolition of controls.
But he said that even without constraints, South African asset managers were unlikely to rush to move funds abroad.

De Ridder said an analysis of returns over the past 15 years showed an optimal mix of equity investments would have been 60 percent in South Africa and 40 abroad. For bonds, the mix would have been 90 percent in South Africa and 10 abroad.
"Natural constraints in the interests of our clients would prevent a prudent manager from moving all his assets abroad," he said.
He said a 20 percent foreign investment limit for pension funds and a 50 percent limit on insurance industry equity investments on approved foreign exchanges would be appropriate.
At present South African funds are allowed to swap up to 10 percent of their local assets for offshore investments, under liberalisation rules announced in June.
But the industry still falls well short of this limit, in part because of foreign investors' reluctance to take on South African assets given the volatility of the rand.
Alick Bruce-Brand, assistant general manager for exchange control at the Reserve Bank, said that by the end of October, the bank had approved foreign asset swaps of 20 billion rand.
Business Day reported on Thursday that 13 billion rand of these deals had actually be executed.

Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals recently estimated the total assets of pension, insurance and unit trust funds at some 600 billion rand, indicating that up to 60 billion rand could be available for investment abroad under the 10 percent rule.

Some believe the total is even higher. Andre Swanepoel, deputy executive director of the regulatory Financial Services Board (FSB), told Reuters he estimated total assets of the three sectors at over 700 billion rand.
Manuel raised the prospect of continued prudential rules for funds when he said at a news conference last week that a "modicum" of exchange control might be retained.
Finance Director General Maria Ramos later fleshed out the idea, saying the department was in discussion with the FSB about steps to protect the nation's savings after exchange controls.

Stals endorsed the need later in the same week, telling Reuters that prudential guidelines would have to be assessed throughout the expected four- to five-year process of phasing out remaining exchange controls, which affect residents only.
"We have been using exchange controls for all kinds of purposes and objectives. Now that we are dismantling exchange controls, other purposes must stand on their own," he said.
Certain sectors of the industry already have their own prudential investment guidelines.
For pension funds, the limit on overseas investment was increased last month to 10 percent from 2.5 percent of assets. Total private sector pension fund assets are estimated at 370 billion rand.

Meanwhile, the rules for the insurance industry will change from January 1 to allow the investment abroad, subject to exchange controls, of up to 10 percent of local liability cover, currently estimated at 350 billion rand.

The insurance industry's prudential rules impose no restriction on the investment outside South Africa of surplus funds, which Swanepoel put at 75 billion to 80 billion rand -- although this is still covered at present by exchange controls.

The unit trust industry, with total assets of 42 billion rand, is bound only by exchange control rules, but Old Mutual unit trusts marketing manager Di Turpin said most funds would likely remain based on South African assets.

"The large majority of unit trusts could be classified as domestic...Their foreign investments would be limited to about 15 or 20 percent in terms of their registered investment philosophies," she said.
